(* Two generic declarations whose parameter types exclude each other only read whole, through a static argument that another parameter fixes, there or through a supertype, are a valid overloading, beside a generic or a plain declaration, and each call runs the one its arguments select (overloading.tex, section "Declarations with Static Parameters"). *)

trait P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] } end
trait Q[\T\] end
object Mixed extends { P[\ZZ32\], Q[\String\] } end
object Box[\T\] end

o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\]): String = "oP"
o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\]): String = "oQ"

r[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\]): String = "rP"
r[\U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\U\]): String = "rQ"

trait R[\T\] end
trait SubR[\T\] extends R[\T\] end
object BoxR[\T\] extends SubR[\T\] end

viaR[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: R[\T\]): String = "viaP"
viaR[\U\](x: Q[\U\], b: SubR[\U\]): String = "viaQ"

trait Ring[\T\] end
trait RingZ extends Ring[\ZZ32\] end
trait RingS extends Ring[\String\] end
object Rz extends RingZ end
object Rs extends RingS end

pairOf[\T\](a: Ring[\T\], b: Ring[\T\]): String = "same"
pairOf[\T\](a: RingZ, b: RingS): String = "apart"

plainOf[\T\](a: Ring[\T\], b: Ring[\T\]): String = "same"
plainOf(a: RingZ, b: RingS): String = "apart"

run(): () = do
    assert(o(Mixed, Box[\ZZ32\]), "oP", "with a Box of ZZ32 only the declaration over P applies")
    assert(o(Mixed, Box[\String\]), "oQ", "with a Box of String only the declaration over Q applies")
    assert(r(Mixed, Box[\ZZ32\]), "rP", "renamed static parameters: the declaration over P")
    assert(r(Mixed, Box[\String\]), "rQ", "renamed static parameters: the declaration over Q")
    assert(viaR(Mixed, BoxR[\ZZ32\]), "viaP", "through a supertype: the declaration over P")
    assert(viaR(Mixed, BoxR[\String\]), "viaQ", "through a supertype: the declaration over Q")
    assert(pairOf(Rz, Rz), "same", "two Rings of one T")
    assert(pairOf(Rz, Rs), "apart", "a RingZ and a RingS")
    assert(plainOf(Rz, Rz), "same", "beside a plain declaration: two Rings of one T")
    assert(plainOf(Rz, Rs), "apart", "beside a plain declaration: a RingZ and a RingS")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

\end{description}

\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
\seclabel{revival-notrevised}

No passage that instantiation exclusion or the reorganized numeric types
contradict is known to be unrevised.
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-inference}); the passages that chapter left unrevised, the
sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} by which static parameters were
inferred before the applicability of a declaration was checked and before
declarations were compared, the implicit bound of \secref{type-param}, and the
rule of \chapref{overloaded-declarations} on a naked type parameter of bound
\TYP{Any}, are revised with the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading},
\secref{revival-bound}).
The instance of a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter of a declaration that a call
reaches only by dispatch, where nothing fixes it at run time, is not described;
the rule of \secref{resolving-overloading} is for type parameters (row~446 of the
revival's gap ledger).
The sentence of \secref{where-clauses} that a \KWD{where}-clause variable may
not appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause also refuses a
variable that a constraint fixes to one type; whether it is to be narrowed is
not settled.
The Meet Rule for dotted methods (\secref{more-specific-rule}) asks for a
declaration on the intersection of two parameter types; whether declarations
that together cover the intersection satisfy it too is not settled.
The type of a static call whose argument's static type stands between two
traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses, where its most specific declarations, or a
declaration more specific than them that the call may run, have static
parameters, is not given (\secref{revival-meet}).
Whether two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments
at which they could meet are ones that a bound rules out is not settled: the
compiled type checker takes them to exclude where the static argument that the
two parameter types force is a named type that fails the bound, and not where
it would reason through the ancestors of the parameter types
(\secref{overloading-static-params}).
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range is
settled (\secref{revival-inference}): it converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an
integer numeral does, so the static ranges of \secref{ranges} and the examples
whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds stand as written.
Before the number chapters were revised, this section said:
\begin{quote}
The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
library's nested tower today.
They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
behind it.
Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
\end{quote}

component GenericPairExcludingWalk
export Executable

(* Two generic declarations whose domains exclude over all their instances, or one of which lies inside the other, are a valid overloading, and each call runs the declaration its argument's type selects (overloading.tex, sections "Declarations with Static Parameters" and "Overloading Resolution"). *)

object Red end
object Blue end
object Box[\T\](v: T) end
object Crate[\T\](v: T) end
trait Tag[\X\] end
trait Sub[\X\] extends Tag[\X\] end
object TagBlue extends Tag[\Blue\] end
object SubBlue extends Sub[\Blue\] end
trait Readable[\E\] end
trait Frozen[\E\] extends Readable[\E\] excludes { Thawed[\E\] } end
trait Thawed[\E\] extends Readable[\E\] end
object FrozenZ extends Frozen[\ZZ32\] end
object ThawedZ extends Thawed[\ZZ32\] end

take[\T\](x: Box[\T\]): String = "box"
take[\T\](x: Crate[\T\]): String = "crate"

tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\]): String = "red"
tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\]): String = "blue"

mark[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: Red): String = "box and red"
mark[\T\](x: Box[\T\], y: Blue): String = "box and blue"

pick[\T\](x: Box[\T\]): String = "any box"
pick[\U extends Red\](x: Box[\U\]): String = "red box"

kind[\X\](t: Tag[\X\]): String = "tag"
kind[\X\](t: Sub[\X\]): String = "sub"

copyOf[\T\](a: Thawed[\T\]): String = "thawed"
copyOf[\T\](a: Frozen[\T\]): String = "frozen"

run(): () = do
    assert(take(Box[\ZZ32\](1)), "box", "Box and Crate are two generic objects, so their instances exclude")
    assert(take(Crate[\ZZ32\](1)), "crate", "a Crate runs the declaration over Crate")

content.content:
(*) operators keep rank and size (Vector[\T,n\] to Vector[\T,n\]).  Nothing is lost at run
(*) time, since map builds its result with replica and m + 1.0 is still a Matrix; a static
(*) checker sees only Array[\T,I\], so the rank and size of a sized argument are lost
(*) to it in the result.
opr +[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T): Array[\T,I\]
opr +[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\](y: T, x: Array[\T,I\]): Array[\T,I\]
opr -[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T): Array[\T,I\]
(*) Scalar on the left: y - x is y - e for each element e of x, so 3 - [1 2] is [2 1].
(*) This is the only pair here whose two orders differ: +, MIN and MAX commute, and so do
(*) the scalar DOT and juxtaposition pairs of Vector and Matrix that this block follows.
opr -[\T extends { Number, AdditiveGroup[\T\] }, I\](y: T, x: Array[\T,I\]): Array[\T,I\]
opr MIN[\T extends { Number, StandardMin[\T\] }, I\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T): Array[\T,I\]
opr MIN[\T extends { Number, StandardMin[\T\] }, I\](y: T, x: Array[\T,I\]): Array[\T,I\]
opr MAX[\T extends { Number, StandardMax[\T\] }, I\](x: Array[\T,I\], y: T): Array[\T,I\]
opr MAX[\T extends { Number, StandardMax[\T\] }, I\](y: T, x: Array[\T,I\]): Array[\T,I\]

(** Additive group making use of %+%.  Must define %+% and
    either unary or binary %-%. **)
trait AdditiveGroup[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\] extends AnyAdditiveGroup
    getter zero(): T
    abstract opr +(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self, other: T): T
    opr -(self) : T
end

\subsection{The type of \KWD{self} in a trait with a self-type parameter}
\seclabel{revival-self-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{idn-ref}; \secref{trait-decls}; \secref{methods}.
\item[Change] In \secref{idn-ref}, a sentence after the one on the self-type
idiom: in a declaration of a trait \VAR{T} with no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', and a
self-type parameter \VAR{X}, \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X} in the bodies of
the trait's methods, and the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type \VAR{T} in the
signature of each method declaration.
In \secref{trait-decls}, a paragraph after the one on \KWD{comprises} clauses
defines a self-type parameter: a static parameter of a trait with no
\KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists only ``\EXP{\ldots}'', that is bounded by the trait at its own static
parameters, or by an instantiation of a trait with a self-type parameter that the
trait also lists in its \KWD{extends} clause, with that static parameter as the
static argument for the self-type parameter.
The paragraph requires every trait or object declaration and every object
expression that extends an instantiation of such a trait to be a subtype of
the static argument of that instantiation for the self-type parameter, a trait
standing as the type of \KWD{self} in its bodies, the intersection of its type with the types
its \KWD{comprises} clause lists or with its own self-type parameter, and gives an example marked ``Not allowed''.
In \secref{methods}, a box after the sentence that a functional method's
\KWD{self} parameter implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object
says that the sentence still holds of the declaration's signature.
Each of the three passages has a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 13~October 2026 on the bodies of the self-typed traits,
and its second form of a self-type parameter, through a trait that the trait
extends, follows a default taken under that decision on 14~October 2026.
\library\ declare their orders and their algebra as traits whose static
parameter is bounded by the trait itself, as in
\EXP{\KWD{trait}\;\TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I \KWD{extends} \TYP{Integral}\llbracket{}I\rrbracket\rrbracket},
and give them default bodies that return \KWD{self} where that parameter is
declared, or pass it where the parameter is expected: the team's minimal
complete definitions, such as \OPR{MIN} on \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} and
\VAR{floor} on \TYP{Integral}.
The interpreter runs them; the compiled type checker refused 29 of them,
since it typed \KWD{self} as the trait.
A bound constrains the static argument, not \KWD{self}: an object may extend
\EXP{\TYP{Integral}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket} without being a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and a body that treats \KWD{self} as the parameter is sound
only if every declaration that extends the trait is a subtype of its static
argument for that parameter.
Scala states that rule for its declared self types (``The self type of a class
or object must conform to the self types of all classes which are inherited by
the template'', \emph{Scala Language Specification 2.13}, section 5.1); the revival reads the self type from the bound, which \library\
already write, as the team's compiled type checker reads it from a
\KWD{comprises} clause (\secref{idn-ref}), a reading that the team's gated test
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXX10k.test} pins.
Naden's account of the Return Type Rule (2012) asked that the self-type idiom
become ``a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but
instead only in bounds''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex}, lines 626--630).
The signatures keep the type of the trait because the type group's account of
overloading of 2019 (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, POPL 2019) assumes, for the
completeness of its matching of types, that no declared type holds a type
parameter inside an intersection (pp.~11:21--22), and its Return Type Rule
compares declared domains (p.~11:13): with the intersection in the signatures,
the domains of the two declarations of \OPR{CMP} on \TYP{StandardPartialOrder}
and \TYP{StandardTotalOrder} became equivalent, and the compiled type checker
reported 18 errors of the Return Type Rule that the declarations do not make.
The second form of a self-type parameter keeps valid as written the mixins of
\library\ that the team wrote in 2009, \TYP{ContainmentBySubset} and
\TYP{ContainmentByComparison}, whose static parameter is bounded by the trait
\TYP{Containment}, which they extend at it.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/self-typed-bodies-judgement.md} and

\begin{quote}
The type of \KWD{self} is the type of the trait or object being declared by
the innermost enclosing trait or object declaration or object expression.
\end{quote}
and
\begin{quote}
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait
called, say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises}
clause, and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned

\end{quote}
The paragraph of \secref{trait-decls} is new.
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 486, the end of the
sentence of \secref{methods} that the new box follows, stands unchanged:
\begin{quote}
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] Under route~C a self-typed trait is read by a \KWD{comprises}

A return to that form would need the clause on the self-typed traits of

group's calculus of 2012 does not admit.
\end{description}

\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
\seclabel{revival-overloading}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
parameter type ranges over its instances.
Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
(\chapref{type-inference}).
The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
example.
A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
every call to which the other is applicable, with a box, and the box on Jan's
example in the internal document gives that rule as its reason.
A further revision has that box say that the factory of \library\ gives a
\TYP{Vector} where its type argument is one of the eight number types and a
plain array where it is any other type, \TYP{Number} among them: the factory
called the vector factory at its own type argument, which has no bound, an
instance that the bound of a \TYP{Vector}'s element type refuses
(\secref{type-param}), and it now builds the vector at each number type, so
that a \TYP{Vector} of \TYP{Number}, which is not well-formed, is no longer its
result.
Another revision has the section's existential reduction read instantiation
exclusion where the two parameter types, or their elements at one position, are
or extend instances of one parameterized trait, where it read it only where they
mention one, with a box, and the internal document's box on the questions on
exclusion says the same.
\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and
\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 393--397, in the revival's
repository), which the compiled type checker applies, with two changes to the
checker: the Return Type Rule checked over every instance, and the positional
restriction.
On 28~September 2026 it decided that a coercion makes a call possible and never
changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it, declarations
being chosen on the parameter types they declare and the declaration chosen
being then instantiated.
Neither implementation enforced the sentence: the interpreter has overloaded
declarations with different static parameters since May 2007, the compiled type
checker applies the rules of that paper to them, and \library\ overload across
different static parameters throughout.
The sentence is text of 2009.
The Fortress~1.0 release of 2008 compared generic declarations instead by
using ``their bounds as their supertypes'', in a section whose type relations
``may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine
are implemented'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf},
Section~15.6.1), and the team's unfinished restart of this specification in
2012 dropped the sentence
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick},
lines 100--114, in the revival's repository).
The restart's Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives function types that hold
generic and plain declarations together, as sets of arrow types and universal
arrow types, and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears
in none of its types
(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
553--558, 764--767 and 794--801).
The positional restriction is the compiled implementation's and not the
language's: its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-overloading/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The No Duplicates Rule was first stated on the strict sense of more specific
that the section defines, under which no two declarations are each more
specific than the other, so that it refused no pair, and two declarations each
applicable to every call to which the other is fell to the Meet Rule (row~696
of the revival's gap ledger).
The paper of 2011 defines its relation of specificity without strictness, one
declaration being more specific than another when every type to which the first
is applicable is one to which the second is, and its No Duplicates Rule
``forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 97--108, 158--162 and 184--185);
the paper of 2019 states it as ``Distinct method declarations must have
different applicable sets'' (Section~2.2), and its rules [No-Dup-Not-Less] and
[No-Dup-Not-Gtr] refuse exactly a pair whose domain types are each a subtype of
the other (Section~4.1 and Figure~5).
The restatement follows the revival's decision of 23~September 2026 that the
type group's later word, that paper among it, outweighs the early text; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-popl-examples/REPORT.md} in the
revival's repository.
The revision of the existential reduction follows the paper of 2011, whose
exclusion of two instances of type constructors reads every pair of their
ancestors (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/fig-exclusion.tick}, lines 136--147, in the
revival's repository), and the revival's decision of 17~October 2026 that two
declarations with static parameters exclude each other as the existential
reduction reads their whole parameter types, in both implementations; its
reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-existential-reduction/REPORT.md} in
the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] Declarations of one name may differ in their static parameters,
as \library's do.
The compiled type checker refuses the pair of the Return Type Rule's example,
which it accepted before and whose compiled class then failed verification, and
an override whose return type reorders its static parameters, which it accepted
before and which then failed at run time (row~398).
Neither implementation runs every set these rules allow.
The compiled type checker refuses more than the Return Type Rule where the more
specific declaration's parameter type is an object type, as in

(* A generic declaration whose type parameter is bounded by a trait with a comprises clause and by a bound naming the parameter, beside a declaration on a trait that excludes only the listed types that meet that bound, is a valid overloading, since the only listed type that could meet both is outside the bound, and each call runs the declaration its argument selects (overloading.tex, section "Declarations with Static Parameters"). *)
component OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion
export Executable

trait R[\T extends R[\T\]\] end
trait Z excludes { A, B } end
trait K comprises { A, B, C } end
object A extends { K, R[\A\] } end
object B extends { K, R[\B\] } end
object C extends { K, Z } end

f[\T extends { K, R[\T\] }\](x: T): String = "R"
f(x: Z): String = "Z"

run(): () = do
    assert(f(A), "R", "f(A)")
    assert(f(C), "Z", "f(C)")
    println("PASS")
  end

end
tests=OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion

run

#!/bin/bash
# The count stage with this probe's shadows: the gate's checker-count/run.sh, with the
# shadowed checker sources that shadow.py (beside this script) writes compiled by scalac
# and put ahead of everything on the run's class path.
#
#     explorations/perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/count.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> plain
#     explorations/perf-probes/self-type-exclusion/count.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> full [selfexc] [bounds] [global]
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with the call set up as the fortress-repo skill says. `plain` runs
# the stage as the gate does, with no shadow; `full` adds the full symbolic-operator check
# with crashes caught per name, and the other words the probe's shadows. The scratch
# directory gets the shadow sources and classes, the copy of run.sh (whose one changed line
# puts $EXTRA_CP first on the java class path), and the stage's own scratch under
# <scratch-dir>/d.
set -u
OUT=${1:?usage: count.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> plain|full [selfexc] [bounds] [global]}
SC=${2:?usage: count.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> plain|full [selfexc] [bounds] [global]}
MODE=${3:?usage: count.sh <out-file> <scratch-dir> plain|full [selfexc] [bounds] [global]}
case "$SC" in /*) ;; *) SC="$PWD/$SC" ;; esac
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:-$PWD}
P="$FH/explorations/perf-probes/self-type-exclusion"
mkdir -p "$SC/ocsrc" "$SC/occlasses" || exit 1
rm -f "$SC"/ocsrc/*.scala
rm -rf "$SC/occlasses"/*

## 11. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers 1 to 6.

1. **The split in order (variant B).** Rejected:
   - variant C, which tests `Node` first and skips 213 tests for leaves: 332 s against B's 344 s, one run
     each, within noise; its exactness needs a proof (every node class implements `Node`);
   - the JVM switch alone: 652 s, and a switch every JVM would need;
   - a class-keyed dispatch.
2. **30 cases per method.** The largest method is 4,474 bytes, against the limit of 8,000.
3. **The patch changes the generator and the file it writes, not the file alone.** A build would otherwise
   regenerate the old walker the next time `Fortress.ast` or a generator changes.
4. **An audit by branch index, not by memo hits.** The fix adds no memo.
5. **The test is in Java**, because of the scalac 2.13 limit (§8).
6. **The brief's "distance stage is `tools/count-run/`" read as `tools/distance/run.sh`.** `count-run.sh`
   runs each interpreter test under walk.

**Findings.**
- The interpreted walker (§2.2).
- The shares of the repair (+267 s) and of rung C (+109 s before the fix, +65 s after) (§3).
- After the fix, about 95 % of the component's time is in the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3).
- The checker's output depends on identity hashes (§9).
- The repair removes the distance stage's crash row and adds no site (§6).
- The other methods over the limit are negligible after the fix (§2.2).

**Defects.**
- **The interpreted walker.** My change repairs it (way 1), pinned by `WalkerJUTest`. No ledger row holds it;
  the row to write:
  - claim: the generated `Walker.walk` (`FortressAst.scala`, from `ScalaAstGenerator.java`) is 31,704 bytes
    of bytecode, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte huge-method limit, so the JVM never compiles it, and every phase
    that walks a tree runs it in the interpreter;
  - status: NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, closed by the fix's commit;
  - class: implementation gap (generator, speed);
  - spec: silent;
  - reproducer: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`;
  - found by: this probe.
- **The identity-hash dependence.** A note for row 488, with the H runs' commands and outputs (§9).

**Sentences of the specification made false:** none.

**For FACTS.**
1. **The fact.** The generated AST walker's `walk` was one method over HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit, so it ran
   interpreted. With it split in order, the count stage with row 680's repair takes 352 s instead of 911 s,
   and the distance stage 931 s instead of 2,375 s, with identical output.
   - What it means: row 680's line can land under the 690 s rule.
   - Test: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`.
   - Detail: §2.2 and §6.
2. **The fact.** The checker's output depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence, because AST hashes include
   the `Class` identity hash. One extra identity hash at start reorders the api checks and the members of
   unions in messages.
   - What it means: the stages' outputs can move with an unrelated edit (row 488).
   - Command: the driver with `-Dprobe.hashes=1`.
   - Detail: §9.
3. **The fact.** Rung C's normal form costs 12 % of the count stage before the fix, 19 % after.
   - Detail: §3.

**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**
- Q1: land the walker split as its own rung ahead of row 680's line, or in the same rung?
- Q2: pursue the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3), about 95 % of what remains?
  - Ways: a memo of normalized meets shared across analyzers; fewer reductions in `Formula.and`'s fold.
- Q3: make AST hashing independent of identity hashes (row 488)? That would change iteration orders, and so
  message text, once.

**Commands worked out.**
- **JFR, read without the text dump.** A single-file Java program over `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile`
  aggregates `jdk.ExecutionSample` within an epoch window, by self, inclusive, callers or callees. A frame's
  `getType()` (Interpreted, JIT compiled, Inlined) shows which methods the JVM never compiled.
- **Methods over the limit:** a `java.lang.classfile` scan of `ProjectFortress/build` for `Code` attributes
  longer than 8,000 bytes.
- **The AST generators by hand, in scratch:**
  1. `javac -cp <scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:ProjectFortress/third_party/astgen/astgen.jar -d <dir>/build ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/*.java`.
  2. Copy `Fortress.ast` into `<dir>/astgen`.
  3. From there, `java -cp <dir>/build:<scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:astgen.jar edu.rice.cs.astgen.ASTGen Fortress.ast`. The `.ast` file's `customClassPath ../build` finds the generators.
- **A huge method's compile attempts:** `-XX:-DontCompileHugeMethods -XX:+PrintCompilation`.
- **Moving the identity-hash sequence:** a driver copy that calls `new Object().hashCode()` N times before
  the phases.

## 10. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.**

1. I shared only answers whose computation read no context. This chooses exactness over reach. The alternatives:
   - TypeScript's rule, dualized: a true answer found under the history's cuts is true without them. It shares
     more, but it can change nested answers, and with them the per-analyzer normal forms.
   - Keys renamed apart, plus the variables' bounds, shared across analyzers.
   - Fuel or depth limits, which change answers.
   - Library-side changes: drop `IntLiteral` from `Number`'s clause, or keep `T extends Number`. These change the
     library, not the checker.
2. Only `True` and `False` are shared, not constraint formulas.
3. A hit in the analyzer's own memo counts as a context read. This is conservative.
4. The memo lives on `TraitTable`, behind its own switch, following rung M.
5. The refusal test carries the `XXX` prefix, by the team's convention.

No decision of the curator covers 1 to 5.

**Findings for the record.**

- The slowdown is recomputation, with the numbers of §2 and §3.
- The count stage on this tree takes about 300 s for the base, measured once at load 0.31. That is not "seconds",
  and the base's `checkApi FortressLibrary` takes 74 s under the fix.
- The overloading stage's error order is not fixed between runs (by reading, §7).
- Noticed by reading, not verified: `withClauseParams` decides by name whether a type variable in an excludes
  clause is in scope (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:820`). So an analyzer whose own parameter has the same name as the
  clause's could read the clause through its own bound. The fix counts that test as a context read.

**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**

- Q1: carry the fix as a rung ahead of fork 2's library half, or with it, or hold both until the distance stage's
  remaining gap (1,032 s against 819 s at the landed gate, not a pair) is also closed?
- Q2: pursue the further exact steps of §9?

**Commands worked out.**

- **Compile the fix into a shadow folder.** Two Scala files at once:
  `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d <dir> -encoding UTF-8 TraitTable.scala TypeAnalyzer.scala`.
  Then prefix `<dir>` to the classpath in copies of the stage scripts.
- **Run compiled `.test` files through the harness on shadow classes:**
  `FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "<dir>:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit <absolute .test paths>`.
- **JFR with deep stacks:**
  `-XX:FlightRecorderOptions:stackdepth=2048 -XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=...,settings=profile,dumponexit=true`.
  `jcmd <JVM pid> JFR.dump name=1 filename=...` takes a copy mid-run, and
  `jfr print --events jdk.ExecutionSample --stack-depth 2048` reads it.
  - The default 250 MB cap keeps only the last few minutes.
  - Aim `jstack` and `jcmd` at the `java` process, never at the stage's `timeout` wrapper. A dump aimed at the
    wrapper killed a run.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table was produced, 1 if it could not be. 20 s in the main tree,
# measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The two sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-22 from
# explorations/perf-probes/prelude/, so that the gate does not depend on a probe
# directory: WorldFlip.java (Shell.useInterpreterLibraries() plus
# PhaseOrder.compilerPhaseOrder, both public, which is the world switch without an edit
# to a tracked file) and shadow-src/.../StaticChecker.java, a copy of
# ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/StaticChecker.java with three
# instrumentation points added: it names each compilation unit it checks and prints that
# unit's error count, and it catches the OverloadingChecker crash instead of dying on it.
# It is put AHEAD of ProjectFortress/build on the classpath, the technique of
# perf-probes/prelude/run-all.sh:33-35. A copy of a tracked source goes stale silently,
# so the checksum of the tracked one is recorded here and the table's "#shadow" line
# says whether it still matches.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false, read
# at OverloadingChecker.scala:77), since 2026-09-27 (climb batch 7). The memo is keyed on
# declaration pairs and hides 27 to 35 errors depending on the build order once an api's
# overloading check runs (perf-probes/nat/triage.md section 1; FACTS.md, "The hidden
# layer, classified"); with it off every build gives one count. The table's "#cache"
# row says so. On the tree of 2026-09-27 the count is 62 with the memo on and off,
# because the FortressLibrary api stops before its overloading check.
set -u

% The new self-type idiom
If the innermost enclosing such construct is a trait declaration (for a trait called,
say, `\EXP{T}'), and that trait declaration has a \KWD{comprises} clause,
and `\EXP{U_1}', `\EXP{U_2}', ..., `\EXP{U_n}' are the traits mentioned in
the \KWD{comprises} clause, then the type of \KWD{self} is instead
``\EXP{T \cap (U_{\mathrm{1}} \cup U_{\mathrm{2}}
\cup \ldots \cup U_{\mathrm{n}})}''.
If that trait declaration has no \KWD{comprises} clause, or one that lists no type but ``\EXP{\ldots}'',
and has a self-type parameter `\EXP{X}' (\secref{trait-decls}),
a static parameter bounded by the trait itself at its own static parameters,
as in \EXP{\KWD{trait}\;T\llbracket{}X \KWD{extends} T\llbracket{}X\rrbracket\rrbracket},
or by a trait with a self-type parameter that `\EXP{T}' extends at `\EXP{X}',
then the type of \KWD{self} in the bodies of its methods is instead
``\EXP{T \cap X}'';
the \KWD{self} parameter keeps the type `\EXP{T}'
in the signature of each method declaration,
which overloading and the choice of a declaration at a call read.
\revision{revival-self-type}{The sentence on a self-type parameter is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 gave \KWD{self} the type of the trait
in such a declaration,
so that a method body that returns \KWD{self} where the self-type parameter is declared,
as the default bodies of the orders and of \TYP{Integral} in \library\ do,
was not well typed.
The revival reads the self type from the bound,
as the self-type idiom above reads it from a \KWD{comprises} clause,
and checks the declarations that extend the trait against it (\secref{trait-decls}).
The signatures keep the type of the trait,
so that no declared type holds an intersection.}
%
See \secref{methods} for details about \KWD{self} parameters.
the following object declaration is not allowed:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%object Mark extends Shape[\Point\] end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Mark} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\llbracket\TYP{Point}\rrbracket \KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-self-type}{The self-type parameter and the rule on the declarations
that extend a trait with one are new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 typed \KWD{self} as the type of the enclosing trait,
or, with a \KWD{comprises} clause, as its intersection with the listed types
(\secref{idn-ref}).
The revival also reads the type of \KWD{self} from the bound of a self-type parameter,
and refuses, as Scala refuses a class whose self type does not conform
to the self types of the classes it inherits,
a declaration that does not conform to it,
so that inside \VAR{T} every value of \KWD{self} is an \VAR{X}.}

There are two sorts of method declarations:
\emph{dotted method} declarations and
\emph{functional method} declarations.
Syntactically, a dotted method declaration is identical to a function
declaration.
When a method is invoked, a special self parameter is bound to the
object on which it is invoked.



A functional method declaration has a parameter named \KWD{self} at an
arbitrary position in its parameter list.  This parameter is not given a type
and implicitly has the type of the enclosing trait or object.
\revision{revival-self-type}{In a trait \VAR{T} with a self-type parameter \VAR{X}
(\secref{trait-decls}), this remains the type of the \KWD{self} parameter
in the declaration's signature, which overloading and the choice of a declaration
at a call read; in the method's body \KWD{self} has the type \EXP{T \cap X}
(\secref{idn-ref}).}

"""Make the checker shadows of the self-type exclusion probe from the tracked sources.

usage: shadow.py <tree> <out-dir> [selfexc] [bounds] [global] [keepvar]

Always: the full symbolic-operator check with crashes caught per name, as the earlier
probe made it (perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/checker-shadow.py <tree> <out> catch),
written to <out-dir>/OverloadingChecker.scala.

selfexc  shadow (i). In the overloading check's exclusion test only
         (OverloadingChecker.validOverloadingInner's `oa.excludes(fa, ga)`), a functional
         method of a self-typed trait whose self type was read from the F-bound (P-146;
         FunctionalMethod._selfFromBound) has its self parameter typed C[\\X\\] & X, the
         TraitSelfType that the disambiguator wrote and that FunctionalMethod.parameters()
         makes plain. Specificity, the Meet Rule's meet, the coverage rule and the Return
         Type Rule keep the plain arrow. Edits OverloadingChecker.scala only.
bounds   shadow (ii). The exclusion test (OverloadingOracle.excludes) gains one more way to
         be valid: the meet of the two domains, reduced as reduceED reduces it but with its
         constraint also reading each static parameter as its bounds wherever it stands at
         the top of the body (the body itself, a tuple's element, a member of an
         intersection or union, a self type's parts), is empty. Its constraint is False, or
         each of its disjuncts' forced equalities leaves a body that is Bottom under the
         merged bounds. Adds
         TypeSchemaAnalyzer.meetEmptyWithBounds and edits OverloadingOracle.excludes.
global   with bounds: the bounds are also read in reduceED's own constraint, so that every
         existential reduction (specificity, the Meet Rule, the Return Type Rule) carries
         them. A variant beside the brief's shadows; not one of them.
keepvar  with bounds: withBounds keeps each parameter beside its bounds (X & B, not B), the
         first form of shadow (ii). It reproduces the solver's recursion without end
         (Formula.tImplies and primImp) on an F-bounded parameter; the report's defect.

With -Dprobe.excdebug=true on the checker's JVM, the shadowed exclusion test prints each
pair it decides by the new reading. Each edit must match exactly once, so the shadow cannot
go stale silently.
"""
import io, os, subprocess, sys

tree, out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
words = sys.argv[3:]
selfexc, bounds, glob = "selfexc" in words, "bounds" in words, "global" in words
keepvar = "keepvar" in words

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.
